title: Endianness
summary: Endianness is just the byte order of a multi-byte value in memory — invisible until you cross a boundary between a little-endian CPU and a big-endian network wire.

slides.markdown:
A multi-byte value (a 32-bit int spans 4 bytes) has to be laid out in memory in *some* order — **endianness** is that order. **Little-endian** stores the least-significant byte at the lowest address; **big-endian** stores the most-significant byte first.

The value `0x12345678` in little-endian memory reads byte-by-byte as `78 56 34 12`; in big-endian, `12 34 56 78`. Neither is 'more correct' — it's purely a convention the CPU (and any code reading raw bytes) has to agree on ahead of time.

slides.subTitle: The same value, two layouts
slides.markdown:
Seeing the same 32-bit value laid out both ways makes the difference concrete:

![The 32-bit value 0x12345678 stored little-endian vs big-endian in memory](assets/endianness-layout.svg)

Both layouts represent exactly the same number — `0x12345678` — the bytes are just written to memory addresses in opposite order. Read the little-endian bytes back as big-endian (or vice versa) without knowing which convention was used, and you get a completely different, wrong number.

assets.alt: The 32-bit value 0x12345678 stored little-endian vs big-endian in memory

slides.subTitle: Mainstream CPUs
slides.markdown:
**x86** and most **ARM** configurations run little-endian. One practical reason: little-endian makes truncating to a smaller type free — a 32-bit int's low-order byte is *already* at the same address a smaller 8/16-bit read would use, no data movement needed. Historical inertia matters too: once dominant x86 committed to little-endian, most tooling was built and tested against it.

There's no deep technical superiority here — it's a path-dependent industry outcome, reinforced by decades of x86 dominance.

slides.subTitle: Network byte order is big-endian
slides.markdown:
Internet protocols (IP, TCP, and most binary wire formats) standardized on **big-endian**, historically called **network byte order** — chosen decades ago partly because big-endian is the more 'natural' order to read left-to-right by a human debugging a packet dump, and partly to have one fixed convention so any two machines (regardless of their own native endianness) could interoperate.

This means any little-endian machine (nearly everything today) must **byte-swap** multi-byte fields before sending them on the wire, and swap back on receipt — `htonl`/`ntohl` in C exist for exactly this.

slides.subTitle: Detecting and swapping
Bi-endian architectures
slides.markdown:
A few architectures (notably ARM and some MIPS/PowerPC variants) are **bi-endian** — the CPU can operate in either mode, selected by a configuration bit at boot or reset.

| | Fixed little-endian (x86) | Bi-endian (some ARM/PowerPC) |
|---|---|---|
| Flexibility | None — always one order | Chosen per system, fixed at boot |
| Common use | Desktop/server, simplicity | Embedded/networking gear needing to match a legacy big-endian protocol or codebase |

In practice bi-endian mode is rarely switched at runtime — it's usually a one-time choice baked into a board's firmware, because mixing endianness mid-execution would be a maintenance nightmare, not a genuinely dynamic per-operation feature.

slides.subTitle: Wrong endianness assumption
slides.markdown:
Parsing a binary file or network packet with the wrong byte-order assumption doesn't crash — it silently produces a **completely different, plausible-looking wrong number**. A 4-byte length field read with swapped endianness can turn a small value into a huge one, then drive a buffer size or loop bound incorrectly.

This is why well-designed binary formats document byte order explicitly, or better, include a **magic number**/byte-order-mark at the start so a reader can detect which endianness was used — PNG does exactly this.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: a swapped length field
slides.subTitle: How one wrong-endianness read turns into a crash or a security bug
slides.markdown:
A network packet's 4-byte length field is `00 00 00 2A` (big-endian, meaning 42) but gets read on a little-endian host without conversion:

```
intended value (big-endian read):   0x0000002A = 42
misread value (as little-endian):   0x2A000000 = 704,643,072

allocate(buffer, misread_length)    // tries to allocate ~700MB instead of 42 bytes
```

The read didn't crash or error — it silently produced a *completely different, entirely plausible* 32-bit number. Depending on what that number then drives, the failure mode ranges from an out-of-memory crash (allocating 700MB where 42 bytes were meant) to a genuine security bug (an undersized buffer being allocated instead, if the swap happens to go the other direction, followed by a write of the *actual* intended length). This is exactly why every serious network protocol library calls an explicit byte-swap function (`ntohl`/`htonl` in C) at every wire boundary rather than trusting the host's native order.

slides.sectionTitle: A subtler nuance: bit order isn't byte order
slides.subTitle: Endianness questions that show up inside a single byte
slides.markdown:
Everything so far has been about **byte order** across a multi-byte value — but some formats also care about **bit order** within a single byte or field, a genuinely separate axis. Network protocol specs (like TCP/IP headers) often draw bit-field diagrams with bit 0 as the most-significant bit of the byte, which doesn't match how most C compilers lay out bitfields in a struct (compiler- and platform-dependent, notoriously non-portable).

The practical consequence: hand-rolling a struct with C bitfields to match a wire protocol's bit-field diagram is a well-known portability trap — the *byte* order might be handled correctly while the *bit* packing within each byte silently differs across compilers/platforms. Production wire-format code almost always avoids compiler bitfields entirely for this reason, preferring explicit shift-and-mask operations on plain integers, which behave identically everywhere.
